modules.name: Methods of purification of organic compounds

blocks.title: Core Concepts : Purification
blocks.text: Purification methods are employed to remove impurities and obtain pure organic compounds. The choice of method depends on the physical and chemical properties of the compound, such as solubility, volatility, and thermal stability.

blocks.title: Key Points : Purification
blocks.text:
Sublimation :

  • Principle: Substances that sublime on heating are separated from non-volatile impurities.
  • Suitable For:  purification of camphor, naphthalene, Anthracene, Benzoic acid, phthalic anhydride, Anthraquinone, Indigo, Iodine and solid SO₃.
  • Solid to vapor state directly by heating without passing through liquid state.
Crystallization

  • Principle: The principle involved in this method is impure compound dissolved in a solvent is sparingly
soluble at low temperature, but appreciably soluble at high temperature. Insoluble impurities are separated by filtration. The filtrate on cooling saturated solution, pure compound crystallises out.
  • Process: Dissolve the impure compound in a suitable solvent → Filter → Cool → Crystals form.
  • Suitable For: Organic solids like benzoic acid, sugar.
Distillation

  • Principle: Separation based on differences in boiling points.
  • Types:
  • Simple Distillation: For compounds with a significant boiling point difference.
Example :

Chloroform (BP. 334 K) and Aniline (B.P. 457 K)

Ether (B.P. 308 K) and Toluene (B.P. 384 K)

Benzene (B.P. 353 K) and Aniline (B.P. 457 K)

• Fractional Distillation:
Used if the difference in boiling point of two liquids is less than 40° C. e.g. separation of mixture of acetone (B.P. 330K) and methyl alcohol (B.P. 338K). It is used to separate different fractions of crude oil in petroleum industry.

• Steam Distillation:

This method is used for separation and purification of organic compounds (solids or liquids) which are steam volatile and are insoluble in water. e.g. Compounds which can be purified by steam distillation are aniline, nitrobenzene, o-nitrophenol.

• Distillation Under Reduced Pressure

Principle: Lowering the pressure reduces boiling points of thermally unstable compounds.

Suitable For: Separation of Glycerol from spent-lye in soap industry.

Solvent Extraction (Differential Extraction)

  • If an organic compound in aqueous medium is separated by mixing it in organic solvent in which it is more soluble than in water.
  • Example : Benzoic acid can be extracted from its aqueous solution using benzene as solvent.
Chromatography

  • Principle: Adsorption chromatography is based on the fact that different compounds are adsorbed on an adsorbent to different degrees. Commonly used adsorbents are silica gel, alumina.
  • This technique has two phases
• Stationary phase

• Mobile phase

  • Types:
  • Adsorption Chromatography and
  • Partition Chromatography
Adsorption Chromatography

Adsorption chromatography is based on the fact that different compounds are adsorbed on an adsorbent to different degrees.

  • Adsorbents : silica gel, alumina.
  • Types : (i) Column chromatography; (ii) Thin layer chromatography (TLC)
Partition Chromatography

  • Partition chromatography is based on continuous differential partitioning of components of a mixture between stationary and mobile phases.
  • Paper chromatography is a type of partition chromatography.

blocks.title: Common Mistakes
blocks.text:
• Overlooking the importance of selecting the right solvent for recrystallization.
  • Ignoring the need for proper temperature control during distillation.
  • Misunderstanding the difference between distillation and sublimation.
  • Ignoring the need for proper temperature control during distillation.

blocks.title: Question 1
blocks.question:
Q. What is the basis for the process of distillation?
a) Difference in melting point
b) Difference in temperature
c) Difference in pressure
d) Difference in boiling point
blocks.answer:
Answer: d
Explanation: The process of distillation is based on the difference in the boiling points of the liquids. Liquids with different boiling points vaporize at different temperatures. In this way, the cooled vapors can be collected separately from the liquid formed. Crystallization is also used to separate volatile liquids from non-volatile liquids.

blocks.title: Question 2
blocks.question:
Q. Which is not used as an absorbent in adsorption chromatography?
a) Silica gel
b) Alumina
c) Potassium permanganate
d) Starch
blocks.answer:
Answer: c
Explanation: A good adsorbent requires a large surface area, should be easily available, and should be less expensive. It should also be thermally stable and have high abrasion resistance. Silica, alumina, and starch possess these characteristics, while potassium permanganate does not, so it cannot be an adsorbent.

modules.name: Qualitative Analysis of Organic compounds (Detection of elements)

blocks.title: Core Concepts
blocks.text:
The qualitative analysis of an organic compound involves the detection of all elements present in it.

Elements in Organic Compounds:

Organic compounds generally contain carbon (C) and hydrogen (H). Additional elements may include oxygen (O), nitrogen (N), sulfur (S), halogens, and phosphorus (P).

blocks.title: Detection of Elements
blocks.text:
• Detection of Carbon and Hydrogen
The compound is heated with copper(II) oxide (CuO):

$C + 2CuO \rightarrow 2Cu + CO_2$

Carbon is oxidized to carbon dioxide ($CO_2$​), which turns lime water turbid:

$​ CO_2 + Ca(OH)_2 \rightarrow CaCO_3 \downarrow + H_2O$

  • Hydrogen is oxidized to water ($H_2O$), which turns anhydrous copper sulfate ($CuSO_4$) from white to blue:
  • $2H+CuO→Cu+H_2O
$
$CuSO_4 ​  +5H_2O→CuSO_4 ​⋅5H_2
O$ (Anhydrous copper sulfate becomes hydrated.)

blocks.title: Lassaigne's Test (Sodium Fusion Test)
blocks.text:
Lassaigne's Test (Sodium Fusion Test)

Purpose: Qualitative detection of Nitrogen (N), Sulphur (S), Halogens (X = Cl, Br, I) and Phosphorus (P) in organic compounds.

I. Principle:

• Converts covalently bonded N, S, X, P in organic compounds into water-soluble ionic salts.
    • Achieved by fusing the organic compound with metallic sodium.
II. Key Reactions (during fusion with Na):

• Nitrogen (N):  $Na + C + N\xrightarrow{\Delta }NaCN$ (Sodium Cyanide)
      • Sulphur (S): $2Na + S\xrightarrow{\Delta }N{a_2}S$ (Sodium Sulphide)
      • Halogens (X):  $Na + X\xrightarrow{\Delta }NaX$ (Sodium Halide)
      • Phosphorus (P): (Generally fused with  $N{a_2}{O_2}$)  $\xrightarrow{\Delta }$ $N{a_2}P{O_4}$ (Sodium Phosphate )
      • (Note O, N, S, X come  from the organic compound)

III. Preparation of Sodium Fusion Extract (SFE):

• Fused mass is plunged into and boiled with distilled water.
      • This extracts the ionic salts ($\text {NaCN},N{a_2}S,NaX,N{a_3}P{O_4}$) into an aqueous solution.

• This clear solution is the Sodium Fusion Extract (SFE).

IV. Detection Tests (using SFE):

1. Detection of Nitrogen (N):

• Reagents: SFE + Freshly prepared  $FeSO_4$ solution + conc. ${H_2}S{O_4} + FeC{l_3}$ solution.

• Result: Prussian blue precipitate.
      • Inference: If S and N both present, thiocyanate forms; removed by boiling SFE.

2. Detection of Sulphur (S):

Method 1: Sodium Nitroprusside Test

Reagents: SFE + Freshly prepared Sodium Nitroprusside solution  $\left( {N{a_2}[Fe{{(CN)}_5}NO}] \right)$

Result: Violet/Purple coloration.

Method 2: Lead Acetate Test

Reagents: SFE (acidified with acetic acid) + Lead Acetate solution.

Result: Black precipitate (PbS).

3. Detection of Halogens (X):

Pre-treatment : Acidify SFE with dilute $HNO_3$ (to decompose NaCN  and  $Na_2S$, which interfere)

Reagent: Add $AgNO_3$ solution.

Result:

Chlorine (Cl): White precipitate (AgCl), soluble in $NH_4OH$.

Bromine (Br): Pale yellow precipitate (AgBr), sparingly soluble in $NH_4OH$.

Iodine (I): Yellow precipitate (AgI), insoluble in $NH_4OH$.

blocks.title: Common Mistakes
blocks.text:
• Confusion between Lassaigne's test results for nitrogen, sulfur, and halogens.
    • Incorrect preparation of sodium fusion extract (Lassaigne's extract).
    • Misinterpreting the color changes in tests (e.g., Prussian blue for nitrogen).

blocks.title: Core Concepts : Estimation
blocks.text:
• Estimation of Carbon and Hydrogen :

$\begin{aligned} & \% \mathrm{C}=\frac{12}{44} \times \frac{\text { Weight of } \mathrm{CO}_2 \text { formed }}{\text { Weight of organic compound }} \times 100 \\ & \% \mathrm{H}=\frac{2}{18} \times \frac{\text { Weight of } \mathrm{H}_2 \mathrm{O} \text { formed }}{\text { Weight of organic compound }} \times 100 \end{aligned}$

• Estimation of Nitrogen :

Nitrogen present in organic compounds is estimated by:

(1) Dumas Method

(2) Kjeldahl's Method

(1) Dumas Method :

  • In this method nitrogen present in the organic compound is converted in to $N_2$ (molecular nitrogen).
Carbon and hydrogen present in the compound are oxidized to

$\begin{aligned} &\mathrm{CO}_2 \text { and } \mathrm{H}_2 \mathrm{O} \text {, while } \mathrm{N}_2 \text { is free. }\\ &\mathrm{C}_x \mathrm{H}_y \mathrm{~N}_z+\left(2 \mathrm{x}+\frac{\mathrm{y}}{2}\right) \mathrm{CuO} \longrightarrow \mathrm{xCO}_2+\frac{\mathrm{y}}{2} \mathrm{H}_2 \mathrm{O} \end{aligned}$

$+\frac{\mathrm{z}}{2} \mathrm{~N}_2+\left(2 \mathrm{x}+\frac{\mathrm{y}}{2}\right) \mathrm{Cu}$

• Volume of nitrogen is calculated at STP.

$\frac{P_1 V_1}{T_1} = \frac{P_2 V_2}{T_2}$

• $V_1$= Volume of $N_2$​ gas

• $P_1$​= Pressure of $N_2$​ - Aqueous tension

• $T_1$= Room temperature

$V_2 = \frac{P_1 V_1 \times 273}{T_1 \times 760}$

Calculations of % Nitrogen

$22400 \, \text{ml of } N_2 \text{ at STP weight} = 28 \, \text{gm}$

Vml of $N_2$ at STP weight =  $\frac{28}{22400} \times V \, \text{gm}$

$\%N_2 = \frac{28}{22400} \times \frac{V}{W} \times 100$ Where W: Weight of the organic substance.

blocks.title: Estimation of Nitrogen
blocks.text:
(2) Kjeldahl's Method :

  • In this method nitrogen in the organic compound is converted into ammonia.
$Organic \ compound +\mathrm{H}_2 \mathrm{SO}_4 \longrightarrow\left(\mathrm{NH}_4\right)_2 \mathrm{SO}_4 $

• The resulting solution is distilled with an excess of sodium hydroxide.

$\left(\mathrm{NH}_4\right)_2 \mathrm{SO}_4+2 \mathrm{NaOH} \longrightarrow \mathrm{Na}_2 \mathrm{SO}_4+2 \mathrm{NH}_3+2 \mathrm{H}_2 \mathrm{O}$

• Ammonia gas is absorbed in excess of a standard solution of Sulfuric acid.

$\mathrm{NH}_3+\mathrm{H}_2 \mathrm{SO}_4 \longrightarrow\left(\mathrm{NH}_4\right)_2 \mathrm{SO}_4$

  • The amount of ammonia produced is determined by estimating the amount of $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$​ consumed.
Normality of $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ taken = $N_1$

Volume of $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ taken = $V_1$

  • Estimation of $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ is done by titrating the $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$​ left after absorption of ammonia with a standard alkali solution.
Normality of $\text{NaOH}$ taken = $N_2$

Volume of $\text{NaOH}$ taken =$V_2$

  • The difference between the initial amount of acid taken and that left after absorption of ammonia is the amount of $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$​ used.
Milli equivalent of $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ used for neutralization of produced $\text{NH}_3$​:

$= \text{Milli equivalent of NH}_3 = (N_1 V_1 - N_2 V_2)$

  • 1000ml of 1N $\text{NH}_3$ contains 14 gm Nitrogen
  • $(N_1 V_1 - N_2 V_2)$ ml of 1N $\text{NH}_3$​ contain $= \frac{14}{1000} \times (N_1 V_1 - N_2 V_2) \, \text{gm N}_2$
Then $\% \text{N} = \frac{\frac{14}{1000} \times (N_1 V_1 - N_2 V_2)}{W} \times 100$

Then $\% \text{N} = \frac{1.4}{W} \times (N_1 V_1 - N_2 V_2)$

W: Mass of the organic substance in grams.

blocks.title: Estimation of Halogens
blocks.text:
Carius Method: Estimation of Halogens

$\% \text{Halogen} = \frac{\text{Atomic weight of halogen}}{\text{Mol. weight of silver halide}} \times \frac{\text{Weight of silver halide formed}}{\text{Weight of organic compound}} \times 100$

$\begin{aligned} & \% \mathrm{Cl}=\frac{35.5}{143.5} \times \frac{\text { Weight of } \mathrm{AgCl} \text { formed }}{\text { weight of organiccompound }} \times 100 \\ & \% \mathrm{Br}=\frac{80}{188} \times \frac{\text { Weight of } \mathrm{AgBr} \text { formed }}{\text { weight of organiccompound }} \times 100 \\ & \% \mathrm{I}=\frac{127}{235} \times \frac{\text { Weight of } \mathrm{Agl} \text { formed }}{\text { weight of organiccompound }} \times 100 \end{aligned}$

$m_1$=  mass of carbon dioxide

blocks.title: Example : Dumas Method
blocks.question: Q. In Dumas’ method for estimation of nitrogen, 0.3g of an organic compound gave 50mL of nitrogen collected at 300K temperature and 715mm pressure. Calculate the percentage composition of nitrogen in the compound. (Aqueous tension at 300K=15 mm)
blocks.answer:
Volume of nitrogen collected at 300 K and 715 mm pressure is 50 mL.

Actual pressure = 715-15 = 700 mm

$\text { Volume of nitrogen atSTP }= \frac{273 \times 700 \times 50}{300 \times 760}=41.9mL$

$22,400 \mathrm{~mL} \text { of } \mathrm{N}_2 \text { at STP weighs }=28 \mathrm{~g}$

$\begin{aligned} & 41.9 \mathrm{~mL} \text { of nitrogen weighs }=\frac{28 \times 41.9}{22400} \mathrm{~g} \\ & \begin{aligned} \text { Percentage of nitrogen } & =\frac{28 \times 41.9 \times 100}{22400 \times 0.3} \\ & =17.46 \% \end{aligned} \end{aligned}$

blocks.title: Example : Carius Method
blocks.question: Example : In Carius method of estimation of halogen, 0.15 g of an organic compound gave 0.12 g of AgBr. Find out the percentage of bromine in the compound?
blocks.answer:
Solution:$\text { Molar mass of } \mathrm{AgBr}$

$\begin{aligned} & =108+80 \\ & =188 \mathrm{~g} \mathrm{~mol}^1 \end{aligned}$

$188 \mathrm{~g} \text { AgBr contains } 80 \mathrm{~g} \text { bromine }$

$0.12 \mathrm{~g} \mathrm{AgBr} \text { contains } \dfrac{80 \times 0.12}{188} \mathrm{~g} \text { bromine }$

$\text { Percentage of bromine }=\dfrac{80 \times 0.12 \times 100}{188 \times 0.15}$  $=34.04 \%$

blocks.title: Example : Sulphur Estimation
blocks.question: Q. In sulphur estimation, 0.157 g of an organic compound gave 0.4813 g of barium sulphate. What is the percentage of sulphur in the compound?
blocks.answer:
$\text { Molecular mass of } \mathrm{BaSO}_4=137+32+64=233g$

$233 \mathrm{~g} \mathrm{BaSO}_4 \text { contains } 32 \mathrm{~g} \text { sulphur }$

$\begin{aligned} & 0.4813 \mathrm{~g} \mathrm{BaSO}_4 \text { contains } \frac{32 \times 0.4813}{233} \mathrm{~g} \\ & \mathrm{~g} \text { sulphur } \end{aligned}$

$\begin{aligned} \text { Percentage of sulphur } & =\frac{32 \times 0.4813 \times 100}{233 \times 0.157} \\ & =42.10 \% \end{aligned}$

blocks.title: Detection of Elements
blocks.text:
• Detection of Carbon and Hydrogen
The compound is heated with copper(II) oxide (CuO):

$C + 2CuO \rightarrow 2Cu + CO_2$

Carbon is oxidized to carbon dioxide ($CO_2$​), which turns lime water turbid:

$​ CO_2 + Ca(OH)_2 \rightarrow CaCO_3 \downarrow + H_2O$

  • Hydrogen is oxidized to water ($H_2O$), which turns anhydrous copper sulfate ($CuSO_4$) from white to blue:
  • $2H+CuO→Cu+H_2O
$
$CuSO_4 ​  +5H_2O→CuSO_4 ​⋅5H_2
O$ (Anhydrous copper sulfate becomes hydrated.)
